chunks: Why the ground loop should be small. The question: Why should your ground loop be as small as possible?
A small measurement loop gives a truer picture. The loop is part of the circuit you are measuring, and its size sets how much it distorts the result.
A larger loop rings more after a fast edge, picks up more stray magnetic noise, and shares more copper with other currents. All three errors shrink when the loop shrinks.
Think of holding a hula hoop in the rain. A big hoop catches far more rain than a small ring. Now imagine the rain is the changing magnetic field around a nearby switching wire.
A big measurement loop catches a lot of it, and that shows up as a voltage on your screen.
One limit: real magnetic fields are not even, so the numbers below are rough estimates, but the trend holds.
Overshoot stays under about 2% for lead inductance up to about 10 nanohenries (ζ about 0. 8).
By 15 nanohenries it is about 7%, and it climbs steeply as the lead grows (30% at 50 nanohenries, 52% at 150 nanohenries). The curve is the probe artifact, not the circuit's.
Drag the probe capacitance down to 5 picofarads: the whole curve shifts to the left, so even a 10 nanohenries lead overshoots by about 12%.
Loop area: the area enclosed by the measurement path; more area catches more magnetic field. Inductance: a wire's resistance to fast changes in current; it grows with loop size.
Ringing: the wobble after a fast edge, caused by inductance and the probe's small charge storage (capacitance) together. Rise time: how long an edge takes to go from low to high.
Pickup: noise voltage induced in the loop by nearby changing currents.
Suppose a nearby wire 5 cm away carries 100 milliamps that switches in 5 nanoseconds.
A loop of 10 cm by 2 cm, which is 2,000 mm², would pick up about 160 millivolts in a rough estimate. A loop of 5 mm by 5 mm, which is 25 mm², would pick up about 2 millivolts.
The area ratio is 80, so the pickup drops by 80 times. You would think you had a noise problem with the big loop and none with the small one. That is the whole idea.
"Because the loop is part of the measurement.
Its inductance, about 1 nanohenries per mm, rings with the probe's capacitance (130 megahertz for a 150 nanohenries clip lead) and distorts fast edges.
Its area picks up magnetic fields in proportion to area, so a loop 80 times bigger sees 80 times more noise from a nearby switch node.
A longer return also shares copper with other currents and radiates and receives more. Small loop, accurate waveform."
Quick check. Which statement best explains why a small probe ground loop is preferred?
